angle: The issue where the evidence contract completed its arc — the checker refuted the database's two-card infinite, verified the real three-card engine, killed the mana-positive hope, then stamped a complete one-turn table-kill with an exact ledger — and the pilot's five approved swaps answered the kill's one verified weakness before the ink dried.

cover.dominant_coverline: FIFTEEN CASTS TO A DEAD TABLE
teases: REFUTED, VERIFIED, LETHAL: six case files walk one engine from database myth to rules-stamped execution
GRAND ABOLISHER: the swap that closes every window the kill opens
THE REBUILD, MEASURED: wincon access 50.1% by turn 6 — the closing speed v2 paid is bought back
NINE GAME CHANGERS: Drannith Magistrate joins, and the floor-4 conversation is honest twice over

departments.note: Heliod at hero scale from the pilot's actual printing (Victor Adame Minguez, MOM 17) — credit line under the art per the featured-artist convention. Tagline 'Everyone draws. Everyone pays.' stays directly under the deck name. This is Vol. 004 regenerated in place for the v3 build (HISTORY.md third entry, sha fbbb52c8): the cover now sells the completed arc — the deck the database was wrong about is the deck with a rules-stamped one-turn table-kill. Every promise above is checker-passed (stacks 001, 004, 005, 006) or a committed artifact figure. Do not add a third violator, and do not tease the unverified candidates: the Archive-halved ledger, the Drannith stranding lock, and the Jace self-deck win are 'needs a stack scenario' everywhere they appear.

Two-bucket contents plus the tier legend printed in full — Vol. 004 updated twice, but every issue is somebody's first. In THIS ISSUE'S DECK, the one-line promise for The Kill should read 'one verified table-kill, two famous fakes' so the arc is promised from page two. The contents blurb for By the Numbers may note the rebuild: same volume, five approved swaps, fresh 10,000-game simulation on the new sha.

departments.headline: THE GENEROSITY TRAP
departments.dek: Why would a control deck hand every opponent an extra card, every turn, on purpose — and then add a rabbit who gives them life too? Because in this court the cards aren't a gift, they're evidence, the sentence is read at each opponent's upkeep — and as of this printing, the execution is scheduled too.

callouts.title: LOOK LIKE A GIFT
callouts.text: Turns one through three are Remora into rock into Kami — or Kwain, whose tap hands everyone a card and a life and makes the whole table like you. Eighteen lands plus a load-bearing rock suite keep you on schedule while the pod files you under harmless, and every card an opponent accepts inches them toward the punisher thresholds.

callouts.title: LAND THE HINGE
callouts.text: Heliod arrives on turn 4 in the majority of simulated games — 5,019 of 10,000 on turn 4 exactly, 89.8% by turn 6. The front face rebuys an enchantment on arrival; the {3}{U/P} flip into the Warped Eclipse is the moment the deck turns on, and it can only ever happen at sorcery speed.

callouts.title: OPEN THE COURT
callouts.text: The Warped Eclipse grants everything flash and discounts your spells {1} for each card your opponents drew this turn. Your own Mines pay your mana bill — and the hug layer feeds it on demand: a Kwain activation or a Second Doctor end-step offer grows the discount on exactly the turn you want to act.

callouts.title: PASS SENTENCE — OR EXECUTE
callouts.text: The punishers convert hand size into upkeep damage: once Forced Fruition fills a hand, cleanup trims it to exactly seven and the next upkeep costs them 7, verified and repeating without you tapping a land. And the deck now holds something no earlier printing of this issue could promise: a checker-stamped one-turn table-kill. The moment Hullbreaker Horror, both rocks, and Aetherflux Reservoir line up behind a Grand Abolisher, you stop playing fair.

captions.Howling Mine: **THE BAIT:** an extra card for everyone at each draw step. Perfectly symmetric on its face — the punishers and Heliod's discount are what make it yours.
captions.Kwain, Itinerant Meddler: **THE HANDSHAKE:** everyone draws, drawers gain a life, and the table likes you — while every accepted card feeds the punisher math and Heliod's discount. Two mana buys the waiting turns this deck lives on.
captions.Forced Fruition: **THE DETONATOR:** every opponent spell becomes seven forced draws. Nobody stays under the punisher threshold once this resolves.

pilot_tips.text: Check your opener for Leyline of Anticipation — it comes down free before turn one and makes every engine piece a flash play, which is Heliod's back face a full three turns early.

departments.pull_quote: The cards aren't a gift. They're evidence.

departments.headline: THEIR DRAWS, YOUR DISCOUNT
departments.dek: Your commander is the one card you are guaranteed to have — so what is that worth when the card is a hinge the whole deck turns on? Here, it is the single most reliable event in 10,000 simulations, and the tax math has a wrinkle no other deck in this series has had.
departments.body: Start with the guarantee. The command zone means Heliod is not a card you hope to draw: he is face up before the first mulligan is offered, and the simulator confirms what guaranteed access is worth — mean cast turn 4.144, median 4, down by turn 6 in 89.8% of games, the most dependable number in the whole issue. That is why Keep or Ship never asks your opening hand for a commander, an engine payoff, or a win condition: the deck's hinge is already on the table, and your seven cards only need to buy the turns before him. The tax ladder reads 4, then 6, then 8, then 10 — but this commander's real recast cost is the wrinkle: Heliod always returns front-face-up, so every recast is tax PLUS another {3}{U/P} PLUS another sorcery-speed window you may never safely get. That math is why protection beats recasting here more decisively than usual — and in the v3 list the insurance is countermagic, not equipment: free or cheap interaction is in hand by turn 6 in 62% of games, and the Phyrexian pip is itself a sequencing lever, because paying the flip with 2 life instead of {U} keeps a whole Counterspell live through the one activation this deck can never take reactively. Color identity is its own lesson: the front face is mono-white, but a double-faced card's identity is the union of its faces, and the blue back face is the entire reason this is a WU deck — the operating color too: 57 blue pips across 38 cards against 16 white pips across 14, with six blue-producing lands against a source target of 36, which is why the rocks and duals carry the deck. The 21-damage clock, for once, is a coincidence: a 4/4 needs six connections and this deck plans zero of them. And the political read: the Radiant Dawn resolving next to a Kwain looks like the friendliest board in the format, and the table will treat it that way — but a turn-one Rhystic Study tells every experienced pilot what bracket you actually are, because this list's floor is 4 on the strength of nine Game Changers alone. The zone guarantees the hinge; the format guarantees the tell.

captions.Heliod, the Radiant Dawn // Heliod, the: **THE HINGE:** the front face rebuys an enchantment on arrival; the {3}{U/P} flip — sorcery speed only, 2 life if you're short a blue — makes your whole deck flash and bills your spells to the table's draw count.
captions.Fierce Guardianship: **THE INSURANCE:** a free 'no' while your commander is on the battlefield. An answered Heliod costs tax, another {3}{U/P}, and a sorcery window you may never get back — this counter is cheaper than all three.

pilot_tips.card: Heliod, the Radiant Dawn // Heliod, the Warped Eclipse
pilot_tips.text: Pay the flip's {U/P} with 2 life on the turn you transform — two life out of a healthy total converts directly into one fully live counterspell across the only window where Heliod is exposed.

departments.pull_quote: You are not protecting a 4/4. You are protecting a sorcery-speed activation you only get to take while he lives.

departments.headline: THE SWAPS, MEASURED
departments.dek: Five cards in, five cards out — so what did the trade actually buy? We ran the v3 list another 10,000 times on seed 42, and the ledger answers in both directions: the engine held its gains, and the closing speed the last rebuild paid is bought back.

callouts.title: 73.6% KEEPABLE
callouts.text: 73.6% of first sevens are keeps at 0.331 mulligans per game. Eighteen lands sounds reckless until you see the kept-hand distribution centered on 2–3 lands plus rocks — the mana rocks are load-bearing, not filler.

callouts.title: TURN 4, LIKE CLOCKWORK
callouts.text: The commander histogram spikes at turn 4 — 5,019 of 10,000 games — with mean 4.144 and 89.8% by turn 6. Heliod is the most reliable event in the deck; the plan can afford patience everywhere else because the hinge shows up on a date.

callouts.title: WHAT THE SWAPS BOUGHT: 50.1%
callouts.text: Win-condition access by turn 6 rose from 42.6% to 50.1% — 61.2% ever, mean turn 3.144 — because Jace, Wielder of Mysteries now counts as a standing wincon in a permanent. The last rebuild's honest cost was closing speed; this one paid it back.

callouts.title: THE ENGINE HELD: 41.3%
callouts.text: 'Engine + punisher assembled', the deck's core two-piece, lands by turn 6 in 41.3% of games — 56.5% ever, mean turn 4.154 — up again from 39.6%, and still a minority: in most games you open as a draw-go control deck waiting for the court to convene. The deck is built to be good at exactly that.

callouts.title: SAYING NO IN 73.3%
callouts.text: Free or cheap interaction is in hand by turn 6 in 62% of games and 73.3% overall — nearly identical to the keep rate. Holding up an answer is not a fallback plan; it is the statistically dominant line.

captions.Thought Vessel: **LAB NOTE:** rocks contribute from the turn after they land in this model — and mean available mana still hits 4.12 on turn 4 and 4.761 on turn 5. Heliod on four, the flip on five: the schedule pays for itself.

pilot_tips.text: Lead Ancient Tomb into a two-mana rock whenever the opener offers it — that line is how 28.1% of simulated games put Heliod down by turn 3.

departments.pull_quote: The last rebuild paid for its consistency in closing speed. This one bought the speed back — both deltas printed, no rounding.
departments.note: The stated-assumptions box is non-negotiable and earns its keep twice here: the model simulates resource development, not games — and it does not model cost reducers, which means every number on this page ignores Heliod's discount entirely. The real deck is faster than the chart; the chart is the floor. Say exactly that, in the lab voice. Cite the sha (fbbb52c8) so nobody mistakes these for either previous build's figures.

departments.headline: THE EXECUTION LEDGER
departments.dek: The database's two-card infinite died in file one. What the checker built from the wreckage is better than the myth: fifteen casts, three fifty-point payments, three dead opponents, one main phase — and a two-mana creature, swapped in this printing, that locks the courtroom doors.

callouts.title: THE ENGINE, ESTABLISHED
callouts.text: Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring + Arcane Signet: each rock's cast bounces the other, and tapping each for its mana while the bounce trigger waits keeps the cycle at exactly 3 mana in, 3 out. Mana-neutral, so the cast count is unbounded within one main phase off a {2} investment. FULL DOSSIER: JUDGE'S DESK A-004.

callouts.title: THE CONVERTER
callouts.text: Aetherflux Reservoir turns the count into life: 'gain 1 life for each spell you've cast this turn' means cast n nets +n, so k casts pay out k(k+1)/2 — triangular growth on a loop that costs nothing to run.

callouts.title: FIFTEEN, PROVEN
callouts.text: From 32 life the gains must reach 119. Fifteen casts pay 120 and clear the bar; fourteen pay only 105 and fail. That is the checker-stamped minimum — not a vibe, an inequality. FULL DOSSIER: JUDGE'S DESK A-006.

callouts.title: THREE PAYMENTS, THREE BODIES
callouts.text: The verified schedule: casts 1–6 lift you to 53, and the first 'Pay 50 life: deal 50 damage' drops you to 3 and kills the 26-life seat via state-based actions. Casts 7–12 rebuild to 60; the second payment (60 to 10) takes the 40-life seat. Casts 13–15 reach 52; the third (52 to 2) takes the last — and with every opponent gone, you win on the spot, alive at 2.

callouts.title: THE VERIFIED WEAKNESS
callouts.text: The same case file names the flaw: every loop cast and every activation opens a fully open priority window. Activating an ability is not casting a spell, so Hullbreaker never triggers on it, and the sorcery-speed loop pieces can only be cast with the stack empty — the engine cannot respond to anything, ever.

callouts.title: THE DOORMAN
callouts.text: Grand Abolisher joined the 99 for exactly that hole: during your turn, opponents can't cast spells or activate abilities of artifacts, creatures, or enchantments — the named answer to the windows the kill opens. Cast it first on the commit turn: its cast is #1 on the Reservoir's own ledger, and the only interactable moment left is the response to Abolisher itself, while the expensive pieces are still safe in hand.

callouts.title: PLANS B AND C, ALSO STAMPED
callouts.text: Approach of the Second Sun's second cast wins during resolution — the only window is while it sits on the stack, and the case file plays out the counter-war, Swan Song included (A-002). And the punisher clock still runs the long game: Forced Fruition fills a hand, cleanup trims it to seven, and the next upkeep costs 7 without you tapping a land (A-003).

callouts.title: TWO FAMOUS FAKES
callouts.text: The refutation pair remains the credibility page: A-001 kills the two-card 'infinite' 296,000 database decks believe in — the Horror's trigger locks its target while Sol Ring is still a spell — and A-005 kills our own hope that Displacer Kitten makes the loop mana-positive: blink and bounce are mutually exclusive on every cast, and the Kitten's best trick is a one-time exit worth 3 floating mana.

captions.Hullbreaker Horror: **THE SPINE:** an uncounterable flash 7/8 whose cast trigger runs the whole engine — and gives the kill zero protection, because activating the Reservoir is not casting.
captions.Aetherflux Reservoir: **THE CONVERTER:** cast n nets +n life, and 'Pay 50 life: deal 50 damage' is paid before anyone can respond. Fifteen casts from 32 life is the proven minimum.
captions.Arcane Signet: **CAST #1:** in the verified walk the humble Signet opens the ledger — its cast bounces Sol Ring, its tap keeps the cycle at exactly 3-in, 3-out.
captions.Grand Abolisher: **THE DOORMAN:** two mana closes every priority window the kill opens — for your whole turn. The swap this printing exists to document.
captions.Approach of the Second Sun: **THE CLEAN EXIT:** the win is checked mid-resolution, not by state-based action, and the first casting counts even though the card was shuffled away. Once every player passes on the second cast, nothing stops it.
captions.Displacer Kitten: **THE HOPE, AUDITED:** every noncreature cast blinks something — but never the thing the Horror is already bouncing. The loop stays 3-in, 3-out, and unbounded mana does not exist.

pilot_tips.text: Lead the commit turn with Grand Abolisher, not the turn before — telegraphed a rotation early he is removal bait and an announcement; cast first on the go turn he closes the windows, counts toward the ledger, and leaves only his own response window open.

Recount the minimum from your actual life before you go: the gains must reach 151 minus your life total, so 15 casts at 32 life becomes 16 at 20 and 17 at 8 — every point of chip damage you absorbed is another cast on the bill.
Hold Swan Song for the counter-war on the second Approach — a 2/2 Bird is a bargain against winning the game, and the case file shows exactly where it slots into the stack.

departments.pull_quote: Fourteen casts pay 105 and fail. Fifteen pay 120. The difference between a threat and a kill is an inequality, and the checker signed it.
departments.note: A-006 is the marquee spread and gets the most ambitious layout of the volume: the full execution ledger as the scene, the three payments as the numbered sequence, the open-window caveat printed beside the payoff — the verified weakness is part of the verified fact, never a footnote. A-004 runs second as the engine room, A-002 third, A-003 fourth, then the refutation pair A-001 + A-005 as the linked double spread. Citations stay in Judge's Desk; this department narrates. Two tier-discipline flags: the Abolisher-closes-the-windows claim rides stack 006's own steps and oracle text, but whether the shield is airtight — the channel-lands loophole, Otawara activating from hand — has no walkthrough yet, so any 'uninterruptable' phrasing must be coach-voiced, not stamped. And the Alhammarret's Archive doubled-ledger extension is a flagged candidate, not a fact: the printed minimum is 15.

departments.headline: EVERYONE KNOWS THE MATH
departments.dek: At a bracket-4 table your Rhystic Study is priced in and your Sol Ring is furniture — so which card on your board actually announces the kill, and why is the right answer to keep it in your hand until the turn it wins?

callouts.title: THREAT WINDOW
callouts.text: Aetherflux Reservoir next to Hullbreaker Horror is the loudest board state you can present: anyone who has done the reading runs stack 006's arithmetic on sight — mana-neutral loop, triangular life, three 50-point payments, dead table — and every removal spell and counter in the pod turns toward you that instant. Hullbreaker alone reads as a flash fatty; the rocks read as furniture. The Reservoir is the tell, so it is the LAST piece you deploy — on the commit turn itself, never a turn early to 'develop.'

callouts.title: THE ONE DELIBERATE TELEGRAPH
callouts.text: There is exactly one board where an early Reservoir is right: the punisher clock already public — stack 003's upkeep arithmetic on the table — and free counters in hand. Then the visible Reservoir soaks the artifact removal that would otherwise dismantle Iron Maiden or the Mine layer, and the archenemy mantle freezes a pod whose upkeeps are bleeding. That is embracing the threat on your terms. Every other early Reservoir is donating information.

callouts.title: ABOLISHER GOES FIRST
callouts.text: The commit turn is now this deck's central play skill, and the sequencing rule is strict: Grand Abolisher is cast ON the go turn, as its first spell — not the turn before, whatever your instincts say about setup. A telegraphed Abolisher sitting through a full rotation is removal bait and an announcement; cast first on the go turn he closes every window for the rest of the turn, counts as cast #1 toward the ledger, and exposes only his own response window while the expensive pieces are still in hand.

callouts.title: SCAN BEFORE YOU GO
callouts.text: Two classes of card beat Abolisher because they are not responses: a Rule of Law-class static already on the battlefield ends a 15-cast line outright, and a Thalia- or Trinisphere-class tax breaks the loop's verified mana-neutrality. Scan the table for those BEFORE the commit. And respect the ugliest out: the verified ledger has you at 3 life after the first payment, so a damage-redirect effect in an open window kills YOU with your own Reservoir.

callouts.title: THE NINTH GAME CHANGER
callouts.text: Drannith Magistrate carries its own political mass. Cast turn 2 into a fresh pod, it unites three commander-dependent players against you for no return; cast when one commander is the table's shared problem, it is coalition glue two opponents will actively protect. Treat it as both magnet and bargaining chip — and don't promise anyone the stranding lock with Verdict or Path, because no stack has walked it.

captions.Aetherflux Reservoir: **THE SANDBAG:** the one card on your board that does stack 006's math out loud. It stays in hand until the turn it wins.
captions.Rhystic Study: **PRICED IN:** turn-2 Study draws groans, not removal, at this tier — but it tells every experienced pilot what the hug costume is hiding: a nine-Game-Changer, floor-4 list.
captions.Jace Beleren: **THE GIFT THAT TICKS:** the +2 hands every player a card and reads as generosity — while feeding Heliod's discount and the punisher thresholds from three opponents at once, behind loyalty no creature wrath touches.

pilot_tips.text: In the control mirror, say 'it can't be countered' out loud before you need it — the uncounterable wrath is a political instrument that redirects the board-committing player's aggression somewhere else.
Spend Teferi's Protection on the Farewell-class sweeper, not the alpha strike — it phases out your entire punisher board, which is the asset the attack was never going to touch.

departments.pull_quote: Every other early Reservoir is donating information.

departments.headline: TWO TABLES, NO TAKEBACKS
departments.dek: One turn asks whether generosity is safe with a spellslinger across the table; the other asks when a god should change faces. Read each board, commit out loud, and only then read the bench's ruling.

callouts.title: HOW TO PLAY ALONG
callouts.text: Cover the recommendation box with your hand. Read the board, pick a branch, say it out loud — the signals and coalition risks are printed with each branch precisely so you can argue with them. Being wrong on this page is free; being wrong at the table costs a game.

pilot_tips.text: Deploy Dictate of Kruphix at the end of the turn before the upkeep you most want taxed — flash means the extra draws start exactly where you point them.
Use Folio of Fancies' X-activation as a precision tool: push exactly the hand you want over seven, exactly when the punishers are about to ask.

departments.pull_quote: The flip is the one action this deck can never take reactively. Its risk compounds every cycle it waits.
departments.note: Two spreads from the decision artifacts: 001 (turn 6 — does Forced Fruition come down against a spellslinger?) and 002 (turn 7 — when does Heliod become the Warped Eclipse?). Both were re-authored against the v3 build and cite the current fbbb52c8 goldfish figures — render them as current, verbatim. The recommendation must sit visually below the branches in both; neither dek nor headline may hint at the answers.

departments.headline: WHO BREAKS THE COURT
departments.dek: Creature wraths hit almost nothing you care about — with one seven-mana exception you must never block with — and the scariest cards against you now are the ones that never use the stack at all. Can you name them before you sit down?

threats.read: Still the one. Your draw engines, all three punishers, the rocks, and the Reservoir sit in a single blast radius, while creature wraths hit a mean of 1.502 bodies by turn 6. V3 made the long game sweep-layered on purpose: Jace Beleren, Jace, Wielder of Mysteries, and Teferi, Temporal Pilgrim survive every Supreme Verdict — including YOURS, which you can cast through their open permission. The new discipline: Hullbreaker Horror is a combo piece first and a blocker never — a wrath that takes an early 'value' Horror costs you the verified kill, not a 7-drop. Deploy in layers, and keep the kill pieces in hand until the commit turn.
outs: Heliod, the Radiant Dawn // Heliod, the Warped Eclipse

threats.read: Ordinary soft locks you now RACE — the kill needs the four pieces and {2}, nothing more. But two classes beat the line structurally, not interactively: a Rule of Law-class effect caps a 15-cast turn dead, and a per-spell tax breaks the loop's verified mana-neutrality. Against those your role flips to beatdown on the lock itself — answer the compounding second piece, not the first inconvenience: a lone Thalia is an annoyance; Thalia plus Deafening Silence is a funeral. And you are now partly the denial player: Drannith Magistrate shuts off every commander and every non-hand cast, which in commander-dependent pods makes YOU the lock. Heliod's discount is the tax rebate no other deck gets.

The polarity flipped: with a verified 15-cast kill behind Abolisher's closed windows and wincon access in 50.1% of games by turn 6, you are frequently the faster, better-protected combo deck in the pod — and the racer does not durdle. Land Drannith EARLY against a known combo seat: flashback, escape, and cast-from-exile lines all die to 'from anywhere other than their hands' — though not true reanimation, which never casts. Spend the free suite (held by turn 6 in 62% of games) only on the card that ends the game. The standing warning survives every version: the hug layer is a liability here — Kwain stays untapped, and Forced Fruition stays in hand unless a punisher is down and you are the one about to win.

You are the control deck and happy about it: Propaganda, Ghostly Prison, and The Second Doctor's rider are virtual card advantage tripled at a four-player table, and Supreme Verdict resets whatever gets through. But v3 adds a ledger this matchup owns: the kill pays 50 life three times, and the 15-cast minimum is computed FROM 32 LIFE — at 20 life it is 16 casts, at 8 it is 17, each extra cast another window. Every point of chip damage you absorb is combo disruption whether the aggro player knows it or not. Pillow hard, let Kwain and your own setup casts pad the ledger, and go a turn earlier rather than a window longer.

pilot_tips.text: Never flash the Horror in early as value into a control seat — it is the one creature you own whose death costs a verified kill instead of a card.
Against storm and spellslinger pods, hold Forced Fruition all game if you must — seven free cards per spell is a donation those decks convert faster than your punishers can tax it.

departments.pull_quote: Your life total is a combo resource. Every point of chip damage you absorb is disruption, whether they know it or not.

departments.headline: ENGINES, PUNISHERS, AND THE LAW
departments.dek: Eighty-four cards doing seven jobs: feed the table, tax the hand, buy the waiting turns, keep your draws asymmetric, say no, survive the wrath — or execute. The load-bearing cards lead, five of them wearing this printing's NEW chip — and the role histogram famously can't see half the plan.

roster.role: The court: engines that feed the table
The hug fort: gifts with riders
Interaction, resets, and the blink engine

captions.Alhammarret's Archive: **THE RIGGING:** your draws double, your lifegain doubles, and nobody else's do — Kwain pays you twice on both halves, and a first Approach banks 14. Five mana that turns every symmetric engine you run into a rigged one.
captions.The Second Doctor: **HEADS AND TAILS:** no maximum hand size means the cleanup trim never saves anyone from the Maiden — and each opponent who takes the end-step card can't attack you next turn. Heads they can't attack, tails they fall behind.
captions.Drannith Magistrate: **THE LAW:** opponents can't cast from anywhere but their hands — no commanders, no flashback, no cascade. The ninth Game Changer, and in commander-dependent pods, suddenly you are the lock.
captions.Consecrated Sphinx: **THE MAGNET:** two cards to you per card an opponent draws — fourteen per opponent spell under Forced Fruition, and the strongest removal magnet you play.

pilot_tips.text: With Displacer Kitten out, any noncreature cast blinks Remora back as a new object with zero age counters — the cumulative upkeep restarts from nothing. The long-run value line is still a flagged candidate, but the object math is plain oracle text.

departments.note: Rank matters: the verified kill package leads for the first time — it is the reason this printing exists — then the court and the sentence; mana closes. Mark the five incoming swaps (Grand Abolisher, Drannith Magistrate, Jace Beleren, Jace, Wielder of Mysteries, Teferi, Temporal Pilgrim) with a NEW chip. Say the honest structural fact out loud in the intro: 23 of these cards, including nearly the entire punisher core, have no entry in the role taxonomy — anyone judging this list by a role histogram will conclude it has no plan, and the histogram is wrong; the plan is on this page. The sideboard strip renders separately as the 60-entry refactoring pool, now holding the five outgoing cards (Lightning Greaves, Worn Powerstone, Horn of Greed, Brass Infiniscope, Monastery Mentor) — label it as the pool it is, per HISTORY.md, and note Upgrade Watch carries the verdict on why each one stays out. Tiles are role-first and carry no printing credits — the physical cards belong to Featured Artist.

departments.headline: A HUNDRED AND SEVEN HANDS
departments.dek: Who leads a credits page with no leader? A hundred and seven artists across 145 entries once the sideboard pool is counted — and the raw top line is half sideboard and one river painted twice. So this issue the feature follows the story: the hand that painted the kill's spine.

featured.note: Two cards, two copies, no inflation — and the two cards are the deck's entire flash-haymaker department: Hullbreaker Horror, the spine of the checker-verified table-kill, and Torrential Gearhulk, the counterspell with a 5/6 attached. In a collection this flat the feature has to be an editorial choice, so we make it honestly: the ranking's top line is Adam Paquette at five entries, but two of those are the same river painted twice — two printings of Prairie Stream — and two more live in the sideboard pool, not the 99, which is exactly why this department reads the table instead of quoting it. Count per copy and you'd crown a basic-land artist: Ron Spears' Island appears eleven times and Zoltan Boros' Plains six — repetition is printing, not authorship, so we count cards, always, and list copies as their own labeled fact. There is no Secret Lair run hiding in these numbers, no collector-number streak, no product bought whole: a hundred-plus artists across three decades of sets, from Mark Tedin's Braingeyser to this year's printings, is what a deck assembled one card at a time looks like. Velinov's Hullbreaker — a leviathan mid-lunge, painted for a horror set and reprinted into this deck's defining case file — takes the hero slot, with the artist credit and printing (INR 68) beneath it, per the convention on every hero image in this magazine.

also_worth_noting.note: Three credits, all of them in the 99: Drannith Magistrate — the ninth Game Changer, arriving in this printing's swaps — beside Metallurgic Summonings and Teferi's Ageless Insight. The largest all-maindeck cluster on the page.

Painted the swap this issue orbits: Grand Abolisher, the two-mana shield that closes the verified kill's windows. His other two credits, Ephara, God of the Polis and Jin-Gitaxias, Core Augur, sit in the sideboard pool.
Two cards, one lineage: Braingeyser and Temple Bell — the game's oldest everyone-draws job and its bell-shaped descendant, decades apart, same hand.

Down to two credits — Fellwar Stone and Mikokoro, Center of the Sea — after the corrected land printings moved the Plains art to Zoltan Boros. Mikokoro is still the issue's thesis painted onto a land: everyone gets a card, and it survives every board wipe in the format.

captions.Hullbreaker Horror: **THE SPINE, SIGNED:** Svetlin Velinov's leviathan is the card six case files orbit — refuted at two pieces, verified at three, lethal at four.

departments.headline: FOUR OPENERS, FOUR RULINGS
departments.dek: The sim keeps 73.6% of first sevens, so the question is rarely whether to keep — it's which of these four you would ship anyway. Rule on each before you read the bench's reason.

hands.why: Three lands, a rock, an asymmetric engine, a table engine, and something that says no — the exact bar: two to four lands, one card-flow piece, an answer. Heliod needs no help from your seven; he arrives by turn 6 in 89.8% of games on his own.

Ancient Tomb into a two-mana rock is the deck's accelerant — the line behind the 28.1% of games that land Heliod by turn 3. Kwain and Jace Beleren both count among the cheap engines worth keeping a hand for: the table draws with you, likes you for it, and feeds the punisher math anyway.

hands.verdict: SHIP — a courtroom with no plaintiffs
hands.why: Three punishers and not one card that makes anybody draw. Iron Maiden against a normal five-card hand is one damage a turn — the punishers are inert until the engine exists, and the full two-piece assembles by turn 6 in only 41.3% of games even from good hands. A hand of punishers and no engine is a mulligan in costume. Ship it.

Three lands and four cards that are all the back half of a game. Nothing here draws, taxes, or says no — and you never mulligan toward wincons anyway: access reached 50.1% by turn 6 now that Jace, Wielder of Mysteries stands in the count, and the four kill pieces are what Long-Term Plans and the 75.7% draw engine find for you in the midgame, never what your opener owes you.

captions.Mystic Remora: **THE UPGRADE:** the card that turns a marginal keep into a live one — a turn-one Remora often banks three-plus cards before the upkeep bites.

pilot_tips.text: Pay Remora's cumulative upkeep two or three times, then let it go — the ages are a fee, not a mortgage, and the cards are already banked.

departments.pull_quote: You are mulliganing toward flow plus interaction — never toward the kill.

departments.headline: THE POOL RUNS DRY
departments.dek: What does a sideboard look like when the deck stops needing it? Two harvest passes emptied this one — the analyst audited every remaining angle against the verified engines and recommended zero swaps. That verdict, the index's leftovers, and the three cards this list hasn't bought yet.

pilot_tips.text: Ignore the index's Sol Ring comparison here — Fellwar's real demerit is the verified one: it sustains the Hullbreaker loop only while an opponent's land can actually produce mana.
The index says Mystical Tutor obsoletes it, but the supersession is narrower than it looks — Plans fetches permanents: a punisher, the Reservoir, the missing loop rock. Keep both.

Do not sleeve the Sphinx as an Abolisher backup — its statics stop counterspells only, a Reservoir activation is not a cast, and 006's open windows are lost to removal and instant-speed plays no uncounterability prevents.

Resist the Greaves return case: it equips only creatures, so it covers Hullbreaker and nothing else in the kill — Abolisher closes every window wholesale for the same two mana, which is why they traded places.

departments.pull_quote: Iron Maiden, Ebony Owl Netsuke, Viseling, Howling Mine, Font of Mythos: zero obsolescence entries. Nothing printed since does this job better — the old cards are the tech, not the debt.
departments.note: Three movements, each honestly labeled. ONE — the index audit: the actionable debt is paid (Worn Powerstone and Brass Infiniscope, the index's two clearest checks, left the 99 in this pass); what remains is nuance — Azorius Signet's Mind Stone entry is a fair swap only if you value the cash-in over colored fixing, Counterspell's 'successors' are conditional counters by their own text, and the incoming five were re-checked: four have no entries at all, and Jace, Wielder of Mysteries' lone entry (Jace, the Perfected Mind) fails the oracle-text test on the only clause that matters — no empty-library win static. Similarity artifacts; say so plainly. TWO — the sideboard verdict, quoted from the analysis: zero swaps, 'the 60 analysable pool cards are now purely conditional tech and spares, which is what a sideboard behind a verified, protected primary line should be.' Run the best of the long-term defaults as fast-facts lines — Omniscience (the pool's biggest unresolved upside, parked until the Approach scenario resolves), Laboratory Maniac (redundancy for a line that is itself unverified), Deluge Virtuoso (zero triggers off an all-artifact loop), Hydro-Channeler (its mana is illegal for every loop piece). Nothing more earns a slot, and this department says so with pride, not apology. THREE — outside the pool entirely: the two-piece rate (41.3% by turn 6) cannot be raised from the sideboard, and the deck-analyst gap study names the consistency ceiling this list hasn't bought — Enlightened Tutor (at the cost of a tenth Game Changer the floor-4 already absorbs), Fabricate, and Trouble in Pairs. Label them deck-analyst shortlist evidence — recommendations, never supersessions. Close on the one real structural exposure, loudly: no Abolisher redundancy exists anywhere in the pool — no other card restricts what opponents may do during your turn — so if the shield is answered, the fallback is the free-counter suite guarding up to fifteen open windows by hand. Acquiring a redundant effect is a decision for the pilot, outside this analysis's constraint.

The Kill is the peak and gets the most ambitious layout of the volume: A-006's execution-ledger spread as the marquee, the engine and the two plan-B lines behind it, and the refutation pair as the linked double spread that keeps the credibility page. Politics (reflection) recovers from the peak, What's Your Play re-engages, Know Your Enemy's four threat-boxes (reference) are followed by two deliberately low-intensity browsing pages — The 99 and the breadth-story Featured Artist, whose pull quote is the issue's quietest page, placed there on purpose. Keep or Ship re-activates the reader before Upgrade Watch, which is light in layout but carries the issue's proudest negative result (zero swaps), and Judge's Desk stays opt-in manila at the back. The completed arc is told at three depths — one cover coverline, the Kill's callout sequence, and the full A-001→A-006 dossier chain — each a level deeper, never merely repeated.
